words.meaning: willing to give and share freely
words.example: My neighbor is very generous, she shares her garden vegetables with everyone.

words.meaning: unhappy because someone else has something you want
words.example: Don't be jealous of her success; celebrate it instead.

words.meaning: changing feelings quickly, often from happy to sad
words.example: Teenagers can be moody, but it usually passes.

words.meaning: worried or nervous about something that might happen
words.example: I felt anxious before the job interview.

words.meaning: not afraid to face danger or difficulty
words.example: It was brave of her to speak up in the meeting.

words.meaning: wanting to learn or know more about things
words.example: My cat is very curious about every new box in the house.
Just be honest with me, I can handle the truth.

words.meaning: able to wait calmly without getting angry
words.example: The teacher was patient while the students tried to solve the problem.
She stays optimistic even when things go wrong.

grammar.title: 3A: Choosing between comparatives and superlatives
grammar.explanation:
Use a **comparative adjective + than** to compare two people, places, or things.

Short adjectives add **-er** (old → older, big → bigger); adjectives ending in y change to **-ier** (easy → easier).

Longer adjectives use **more + adjective** (modern → more modern, difficult → more difficult).

Memorize the irregular forms: **good → better**, **bad → worse**, **far → further/farther**.

Adjectives of character follow the same rules: generous, jealous, stubborn, moody, anxious, brave, curious, honest, patient, and optimistic can all become comparatives.

Use **(not) as + adjective + as** to say things are equal or not equal; use **the same as** for identical things.

Comparative adverbs compare actions the same way: fast → faster, slowly → more slowly, well → better, badly → worse.

Use **the + superlative** to compare one person or thing with the whole group.

Superlatives take **-est** (biggest), **the most / the least** (most modern), and the irregulars **best** and **worst**.

After a superlative use **in**, not of. Superlatives often pair with the present perfect and ever, as in the *most generous* person I've ever met.
examples: My uncle is the *most generous* person in our family. (superlative of a long adjective)
Don't be *more jealous than* you need to be; her success doesn't hurt you.
My little brother is *more stubborn than* our dad.
The weather today is *moodier than* yesterday. (y → ier)
She felt *more anxious than* me before the interview.
He was *braver than* anyone else in the team.
My sister is *more curious than* I am about the world.
Just be *as honest as* you can in the interview. (as + adjective + as)
A *more patient* teacher gets better results *than* a strict one.
Staying optimistic is *better than* giving up. (irregular: good → better)

practice.q: Which is correct: "She is more brave than me" or "She is braver than me"?
practice.a: "She is braver than me" — short adjectives take -er, not more.

practice.q: Complete: "This is the ___ (good) book I have ever read."
practice.a: "the best" — superlative with the present perfect + ever.
